Epoch AI study finds China more exposed to semiconductor supply shocks than US
A simulated disruption scenario points to higher costs and deeper economic losses for China if chip supplies are cut off
If the global chip supply chain seized up tomorrow, both superpowers would feel it. According to new analysis from Epoch AI, China would feel it more.
Epoch AI modeled what happens to each economy when the flow of semiconductors gets disrupted. The conclusion is directional and clear: China comes out worse on both cost and economic damage.
China remains heavily dependent on imports for advanced semiconductor tools and materials. Those are the expensive, hard-to-replicate machines and inputs needed to make cutting-edge chips. US export controls make that dependence more painful. Washington has spent recent years restricting what China can buy, so a supply shock would land on a system that is already constrained.
Epoch AI’s broader work on chip supply chains has flagged three major bottlenecks in AI hardware: advanced logic wafers, CoWoS, and high-bandwidth memory, or HBM. Logic wafers are the silicon brains of a chip. CoWoS is an advanced packaging technique that stitches components together. HBM is the ultra-fast memory that keeps AI processors fed with data. Lose any one of them, and the finished product doesn’t ship.
The smuggling side of the story
An Epoch AI report published April 29, 2026 estimated that somewhere between 290k and 1.6M H100-equivalent chips were smuggled into China through 2025. The median estimate sits at 660k. By the group’s estimate, smuggled chips account for about one-third of China’s total AI compute.
The spread in the estimate is also worth noting. The high end is more than five times the low end, which shows how murky this market is.
AI, tech, and the markets they move—in one daily briefing.
Daily. Free. Join 34,000+ readers across crypto, finance, and policy.
Interdependence cuts both ways
China dominates manufacturing for certain electronic components. The US, meanwhile, controls advanced design technologies and crucial fabrication capabilities. The US depends on Chinese transformers for its data centers — the electrical kind — and the AI buildout can’t run without them.
Taiwan and Hong Kong both show high export dependence on AI-enabling goods, which ties their economic fortunes closely to how the US-China chip standoff plays out.
Epoch AI also tracks who consumes the components that go into AI chips. That work points to heavy reliance on a handful of firms, including Nvidia, AMD, Google, and Amazon, particularly for HBM and advanced packaging capacity.
What this means
The smuggling estimates complicate the export-control story. If about one-third of China’s AI compute arrives through unofficial channels, enforcement matters as much as the rules on paper.
HBM, advanced packaging, and leading-edge wafers are already tight. A shock in any of them would ripple through Nvidia, AMD, Google, Amazon, and everyone downstream who depends on their hardware. The US transformer dependence on China for data centers represents a quieter but parallel risk.

articles.title: Elon Musk says TSMC could join Terafab- What Taiwan chip giant's entry into US market means - Livemint
articles.summary: Elon Musk says TSMC could join Terafab- What Taiwan chip giant's entry into US market means  Livemint
articles.full_text:
Elon Musk has confirmed that Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. (TSMC) could participate in Terafab, the Texas chipmaking venture being developed by Tesla and SpaceX.
The development puts one of the world's biggest semiconductor manufacturers alongside Intel, which was the earliest known chipmaker to back the project, and raises a bigger question: Is Musk building a chip factory, or an entire semiconductor ecosystem for his companies?
Intel shares fell more than 4% in premarket trading on Monday after the development emerged, while TSMC shares rose in Taiwan and in US trading. The market reaction reflects concerns that TSMC's involvement could dilute Intel's expected role in a project that could become strategically important for Elon Musk's expanding technology businesses.
Terafab is a planned semiconductor manufacturing facility in Grimes County, Texas, backed by Tesla and SpaceX. The companies have announced an initial investment of $16.8 billion and a planned workforce of at least 3,000 people.
The chips are expected to support Tesla's Optimus humanoid robots and Cybercabs, as well as SpaceX's ambitions for space-based data centres. Total spending across the project's different phases could eventually reach as much as $119 billion.
Intel has acknowledged a role in Terafab, although it has not disclosed precisely what that role will involve.
TSMC's potential entry changes the picture. Instead of relying on one major chipmaker, Musk could be assembling a network of semiconductor expertise around his companies.
TSMC brings something Elon Musk cannot easily build from scratch: decades of experience in advanced semiconductor manufacturing.
Making cutting-edge chips is not simply about constructing a factory. Process technology, manufacturing yields, advanced packaging and the ability to produce chips consistently at scale are equally important.
Elon Musk's companies can provide enormous demand for chips, while TSMC could contribute manufacturing expertise and Intel could bring US semiconductor infrastructure.
Terafab was conceived as a vertically integrated operation covering logic, memory, advanced packaging and testing. Tesla has also been recruiting semiconductor engineers in Taiwan, including people with expertise in advanced nodes and packaging.
The emerging model therefore looks less like a conventional chip-supply agreement and more like an attempt to build greater control over the semiconductor chain.
Elon Musk's companies are becoming major consumers of computing power, but their requirements are different.
Tesla needs processors for autonomous driving and vehicles. Optimus will require specialised AI and robotics chips. SpaceX has growing computing requirements, including its plans for space-based data centres.
Then there is xAI, whose expanding AI infrastructure requires large quantities of advanced computing hardware.
Terafab could eventually serve these different businesses, giving Musk a substantial captive customer base for a semiconductor operation.
That could also reduce dependence on a single external chip supplier.
TSMC's potential involvement comes as the Taiwanese chipmaker expands its US footprint.
The company has already committed $265 billion towards its Arizona expansion and is considering a separate Texas campus, with each fabrication plant expected to require an investment of at least $20 billion.
TSMC already manufactures some chips for Tesla. Tesla has also signed a separate $16.5 billion agreement with Samsung for its next-generation AI6 chip, according to Electrek.
It is worth noting that Tesla is developing relationships with several major chipmakers while simultaneously seeking greater control over its own semiconductor capabilities.
The potential involvement of TSMC comes as semiconductor manufacturing is becoming an increasingly important part of US industrial policy and corporate strategy.
TSMC, headquartered in Taiwan, is expanding its manufacturing presence in the US, while Intel is investing in its own domestic foundry operations. ASML, the Dutch company whose extreme ultraviolet lithography machines are used to produce some of the most advanced chips, is another key supplier to both manufacturers.
Elon Musk has been seeking support from several parts of that supply chain. Earlier this year, he addressed employees at an ASML technology conference to discuss Terafab, highlighting the equipment the project would require.
The precise roles that TSMC and Intel would play at Terafab have not been disclosed. But their potential involvement would give the project links to two of the world's leading chip manufacturers at a time when Tesla and SpaceX are seeking to secure more computing capacity for vehicles, robots, artificial intelligence and space-related applications.

articles.title: Shionogi Grows Rare Disease Portfolio with $2B IntraBio Acquisition - Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology News
articles.summary: Shionogi Grows Rare Disease Portfolio with $2B IntraBio Acquisition  Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology News
articles.full_text:
Shionogi has agreed to acquire IntraBio for $2 billion, in a deal intended to expand the Japanese pharma’s rare disease portfolio with a drug marketed in the U.S. and European Union for neurological manifestations of Niemann-Pick disease type C (NPC).
The drug, Aqneursa® (levacetylleucine), was approved by the FDA in September 2024 for neurological manifestations of Niemann-Pick disease Type C (NPC) in adults and children weighing 15 kg (33 pounds) or more, and by the European Medicines Agency (EMA) in January.
On September 18, the FDA approved a supplemental New Drug Application expanding the label of Aqneursa to become the first and to date only drug approved for the treatment of ataxia in ataxia-telangiectasia (A-T) patients weighing 15 kg (33 pounds) or more. Aqneursa is now under review by the EMA for adults and children diagnosed with A-T.
“The planned acquisition of IntraBio actively demonstrates Shionogi’s solid commitment to building a leading global rare disease business,” Isao Teshirogi, PhD, Shionogi’s president, CEO, and representative director said Monday in a statement. “Bringing Aqneursa to Shionogi after our acquisition of Radicava® will deepen our commitment to rare disease communities, expand our capabilities and strengthen our portfolio as we advance future innovation for patients with significant unmet needs.”
Investors initially appeared less enthusiastic about the IntraBio acquisition, as Shionogi’s shares traded on the Tokyo Stock Exchange fell about 4.5% Monday, from ¥2,786 ($17.61) to ¥2,661 ($16.82)—but the stock bounced back Tuesday, all but recovering with a 3.8% gain that sent shares up to Y2,763 ($17.47).
However, Sumant Kulkarni, a senior analyst covering biotechnology with Canaccord Genuity, viewed the deal more positively.
“In summary, this transaction underscores our view that companies with approved products for rare indications, neuro or otherwise, present significant scarcity value for strategics and investors alike,” Kulkarni wrote Monday in a research note. “We are not entirely surprised by this development, but are encouraged by the upfront consideration.”
Kulkarni added: “In fact, we were surprised that IntraBio had remained independent for the time it did, but the timing makes sense given the recent approval for A-T, which adds another leg to its story.”
‘Plenty of financial firepower’
The acquisition of IntraBio comes two months after Teshirogi told Bloomberg News in an interview that Shionogi was “actively pursuing” at least three acquisition opportunities: “From a cash flow perspective, we’ve become a company with plenty of financial firepower. If a good opportunity comes along, there’s absolutely no reason for us to hesitate over any M&A.”
Teshirogi also said Shionogi was looking to expand its U.S. and European manufacturing capacity in order to diversify its production base beyond Japan and thus reduce geopolitical risk over the next decade.
To that end, Shionogi pursued and won a U.S. government contract in April to establish a Stateside drug product manufacturing site for its Fetroja® cefiderocol), a cephalosporin antibacterial indicated to treat adults with complicated urinary tract infections (cUTI) including pyelonephritis; as well as hospital-acquired and ventilator-associated bacterial pneumonia (HABP/VABP).
The contract—awarded through the Biomedical Advanced Research and Development Authority’s (BARDA) Project BioShield—was initially funded at $119 million with multiyear options for a total of up to $482 million.
Shionogi signaled its intent to focus on rare disease drugs in April when it agreed to acquire Radicava (edaravone), a small molecule treatment for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), from Tanabe Pharma for $2.5 billion and a potential royalty on future sales. At the time, Shionogi said the deal would benefit it by adding approximately $700 million in annual global sales during the company’s current 2026 fiscal year, which began on April 1.
59% leap
That would represent a 59% leap from Shionogi’s entire FY 2025 earnings before interest taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) of ¥187.72 billion ($1.187 billion), up 4.7% from ¥179.296 billion ($1.134 billion) in FY 2024.
Radicava generated ¥94.491 billion ($597.582 million) in the 2025 fiscal year that ended on March 31 of this year.
“Through this acquisition, the Company aims to strengthen its business foundation and enhance its corporate value over the medium to long term by maximizing the value of edaravone and expanding its provision of solutions in the rare disease area,” Shionogi explained in reporting fiscal Q1 (April-June) 2026 results in August.
Radicava is marketed under that name as an intravenous (IV) infusion, and as an oral suspension called Radicava ORS. The IV version was approved by the FDA in 2022 and the oral suspension version, two years later.
Based in Austin, TX, IntraBio was established in 2015 to discover, develop, and commercialize therapies for neurodegenerative diseases with high unmet medical need, by commercializing research generated by its scientific co-founders—Professors Grant Churchill, PhD, Antony Gallone, PhD, and Frances Platt, PhD, all of the University of Oxford; and Michael Strupp, MD, of the University of Munich.
Privately held IntraBio finished last year with a $35.8 million net loss on net sales of $67.867 million—all of it generated from sales of Aqneursa—according to data disclosed by Shionogi in its announcement of the acquisition.
Shionogi is expected to close on its acquisition of IntraBio during this quarter, subject to customary closing conditions.

articles.title: Cathie Wood's ARK Invest Rotates $22 Million in Biotech, Extends Intellia Buying Streak to 50 Sessions - BigGo Finance
articles.summary: Cathie Wood's ARK Invest Rotates $22 Million in Biotech, Extends Intellia Buying Streak to 50 Sessions  BigGo Finance
articles.full_text:
Cathie Wood's ARK Invest reshaped its healthcare exposure across its flagship exchange-traded funds on Monday, unloading roughly $18 million of Twist Bioscience stock for the 21st consecutive session while pouring fresh capital into Recursion Pharmaceuticals, Intellia Therapeutics and Veracyte.
Across the ARK Innovation ETF (ARKK) and ARK Genomic Revolution ETF (ARKG), the firm bought approximately $15 million of healthcare names and sold about $22 million, according to trade disclosures published Tuesday morning. The activity points less to a retreat from biotechnology than to a deliberate rotation within the genomics theme, with capital shifting toward companies that ARK appears to view as having nearer-term clinical, diagnostic or drug-discovery catalysts.
Recursion received the largest combined allocation at roughly $6.6 million, with about $5.3 million routed through ARKK and $1.3 million through ARKG. The AI-driven drug-discovery company's shares surged more than 16% on Monday, extending a rally that market participants have linked to its recently extended data-licensing partnership with Tempus, now running through 2029. Wall Street analysts hold a consensus 12-month price target of $7.22 for Recursion, according to Koyfin data, implying upside of more than 51% from current levels.
Intellia Therapeutics drew approximately $1.2 million in combined purchases, split between ARKK and ARKG. The acquisition extended a remarkable accumulation streak: ARK has now added to its Intellia position for 50 straight sessions. Since September 29, the firm has bought more than 1.17 million shares across multiple transactions.
The persistent buying comes as Intellia approaches a pivotal regulatory milestone. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has accepted the company's biologics application for lonvoguran ziclumeran, an investigational in-vivo CRISPR therapy for hereditary angioedema, for Priority Review. A decision is scheduled for March 10, 2027. If cleared, Intellia says the therapy could become the first in-vivo CRISPR-based treatment to reach the market.
Not everyone shares ARK's enthusiasm. Barclays recently initiated coverage on Intellia with an Underweight rating and an $8 price target, suggesting potential downside of about 36% from current trading levels. The divergence highlights the binary nature of the FDA decision looming in early 2027.
ARKG accounted for most of Monday's remaining purchases. The fund added roughly $5.4 million of Veracyte, building on a position that ARK expanded earlier in October with about 159,000 shares. The diagnostics company reported 15% year-over-year revenue growth to $150.3 million in the second quarter, with testing revenue up 19%. It also acquired Convergent Genomics in September to strengthen its urinary cancer-testing capabilities. Late last month, Veracyte disclosed Phase 3 data showing its Decipher Prostate test could help identify which intermediate-risk prostate cancer patients might benefit from adding hormone therapy to radiation.
ARKG also made smaller additions to Freenome and Scribe Therapeutics, buying roughly $777,000 and $727,000 respectively.
On the selling side, Twist Bioscience dominated the outflows. ARK sold approximately $18 million of the synthetic-DNA company across its funds, with about $9.5 million coming from ARKK and $8.5 million from ARKG. The divestment of 90,713 shares marked the 21st consecutive session of Twist selling. ARKG alone has liquidated roughly $6 million of Twist stock in recent weeks.
The continued trimming stands in contrast to Twist's market momentum. The stock climbed 8.7% on Monday and has appreciated more than 60% over the past month, driven by enthusiasm around its synthetic-DNA platform and its role in Eli Lilly's TuneLab AI-powered drug-discovery initiative. Twist recently joined the program, providing antibody characterization data to support AI and machine-learning models aimed at accelerating pharmaceutical research. Year to date, Twist shares have surged approximately 533%.
ARK also reduced positions in two other recent winners. The firm sold about $2.6 million of 10x Genomics and $1.5 million of CareDx through ARKG. 10x Genomics gained 4.5% on Monday and has climbed more than 48% over the past month, bringing its year-to-date advance to roughly 499%. CareDx rose 4% to its highest level in more than four years and has gained about 265% in 2026.
The trading pattern reveals a clear strategy. Twist accounted for roughly 80% of ARK's combined healthcare selling on Monday, while purchases concentrated on Recursion and Intellia through ARKK and on Veracyte and other precision-diagnostics names through ARKG. The rotation aligns with a broader pharmaceutical industry shift toward AI-driven drug discovery, precision diagnostics and gene-editing platforms.
For ARK, the emerging question is no longer whether genomics will transform healthcare, but which companies can convert those technologies into commercially viable medicines and diagnostics. Monday's trades suggest the firm is positioning accordingly, trimming positions that have delivered outsized gains while adding to names with defined catalysts on the horizon.
The moves also reflect ARK's characteristic approach of using market strength to rebalance. Twist's 60% monthly surge gave the firm an opportunity to lock in profits after an extended run, while Intellia's 50-session buying streak indicates a conviction that the FDA decision in March 2027 could serve as a major inflection point for the gene-editing sector.
Twist Bioscience and 10x Genomics have been the standout performers in ARK's biotech portfolio this year, while CareDx, Intellia, Recursion and Veracyte have all posted double-digit advances. The challenge for Wood and her team is deciding which of these rallies still has room to run and which has priced in too much optimism.
Monday's disclosures suggest ARK is making that judgment call in real time, rotating out of its biggest winners and concentrating firepower on the names it believes hold the most catalytic potential heading into 2027.

articles.title: CATL vs BYD vs Tesla: Who Leads the Global BESS Market in 2026? - GreentechLead
articles.summary: CATL vs BYD vs Tesla: Who Leads the Global BESS Market in 2026?  GreentechLead
articles.full_text:
The global battery energy storage system (BESS) race in 2026 is producing three different leaders. CATL dominates battery cells, BYD has moved to No. 1 in complete BESS system shipments, while Tesla is relying on Megapack and software-led energy optimization to differentiate itself.
Global BESS cell shipments exceeded 490 GWh in H1 2026, nearly doubling year over year, while system shipments reached approximately 313 GWh, up 93 percent, according to Benchmark Mineral Intelligence.
CATL controlled 22 percent of global BESS cell shipments, versus 6.7 percent for BYD. At the system level, however, BYD ranked first with 9.1 percent, CATL held 8 percent and Tesla ranked fourth with 7.1 percent.
The figures reveal how the global battery storage market is evolving from a race for battery manufacturing scale into a broader contest involving system integration, project execution, software, service and lifetime economics.
Cell and system shipments are different measurements. Cells move through the supply chain before becoming complete storage products, while system shipments represent finished BESS solutions supplied by integrators.
That distinction explains why CATL can dominate cells while BYD leads systems.
CATL Builds Its Lead on Battery Scale
CATL has the strongest upstream position.
Its BESS cell shipments doubled in H1 2026 while it retained a 22 percent global share, more than double the 10.2 percent held by second-ranked HiTHIUM.
Manufacturing scale reinforces the advantage. CATL ended 2025 with 772 GWh of global battery production capacity, with another 321 GWh under construction. Lithium-ion battery sales reached 661 GWh, up 39 percent.
CATL also accounted for 30.4 percent of global energy-storage battery shipments in 2025, according to SNE Research data cited by the company, retaining the top position for the fifth consecutive year.
Its storage batteries have been deployed across approximately 2,300 projects worldwide.
Technology investment strengthens the position. CATL spent RMB 22.1 billion on R&D in 2025 and is expanding beyond conventional LFP batteries into sodium-ion storage.
Its TENER family targets high-density and long-duration applications, while TENER Sodium expands its chemistry portfolio. CATL expects cumulative sodium-ion storage shipments to reach 1 GWh by the end of 2026.
The challenge is downstream. CATL’s 22 percent cell share falls to only 8 percent in system shipments. Its next growth opportunity is therefore turning battery dominance into greater control of complete BESS projects.
BYD Becomes the System-Integration Leader
BYD presents almost the reverse picture.
It controlled only 6.7 percent of BESS cell shipments in H1 2026 but captured 9.1 percent of complete system shipments, ranking first globally.
More importantly, BYD’s system shipments surged 96.6 percent year over year, compared with 68.5 percent for CATL and only 11.5 percent for Tesla.
This suggests BYD is increasingly succeeding at converting its battery manufacturing and vertical integration into complete grid-storage solutions.
BYD Energy Storage combines batteries, BESS, power conversion systems, energy-management systems, service and recycling. The company says it has supplied more than 650 projects across over 110 countries and regions.
Its scale is particularly visible in Saudi Arabia. BYD signed contracts with Saudi Electricity Company covering 12.5 GWh of grid-scale storage. Combined with an earlier 2.6 GWh project, their cooperation has reached 15.1 GWh.
BYD is also increasing system density. Its latest Haohan platform reaches 14.5 MWh, reflecting the rapid technology improvements accompanying the broader decline in battery energy storage costs.
BYD’s weakness is its smaller merchant BESS cell position. CATL’s 22 percent share is more than three times BYD’s 6.7 percent.
BYD therefore needs to defend its system leadership as CATL moves further downstream.
Tesla Faces a Different Competitive Challenge
Tesla remains one of the most important global BESS companies, but its 2026 shipment momentum is considerably weaker.
Tesla deployed a record 46.7 GWh of energy-storage products in 2025, including 14.2 GWh during the fourth quarter.
Its Lathrop and Shanghai Megafactories have combined stated manufacturing capacity of 80 GWh annually, while Tesla is adding Megapack 3 and Megablock production in Houston.
But H1 2026 exposed a challenge.
Tesla’s system shipments increased only 11.5 percent, compared with overall market growth of 93 percent. Its market share fell 5.2 percentage points year over year to 7.1 percent, pushing Tesla outside the global top three system integrators.
Tesla consequently needs to compete on something other than shipment volume.
Its answer is increasingly software.
Tesla Autobidder automates electricity-market bidding and battery dispatch according to revenue opportunities and owners’ risk preferences. Megapack also integrates battery modules, inverters, thermal management and controls into a standardized system.
That makes Tesla’s proposition particularly relevant to merchant projects where revenue optimization can materially affect lifetime returns.
Three Companies, Three BESS Strategies
| Competitive area | CATL | BYD | Tesla | 
| BESS cells | Leader | Major supplier | — | 
| System shipments | No. 3 | No. 1 | No. 4 | 
| Manufacturing | Major strength | Major strength | Expanding | 
| Vertical integration | Strong | Very strong | System/software | 
| Technology | Broad chemistry | LFP/Blade Battery | LFP Megapack | 
| Software | Growing | Integrated EMS | Key strength | 
| 2026 momentum | Strong | Strongest | Weaker | 
CATL is attempting to extend battery dominance downstream. BYD is showing that vertical integration can transform a smaller cell position into system leadership. Tesla is betting that hardware combined with software can create value not captured by shipment rankings.
BESS Integration Remains More Competitive
The battery-cell market is significantly more concentrated than system integration.
The top 10 BESS cell suppliers controlled 83.3 percent of global shipments in H1 2026, and all ten were Chinese companies.
By comparison, the top 10 system integrators accounted for only 60 percent of shipments, down 16.8 percentage points from the previous year. Tesla was the only non-Chinese company among the top ten.
This fragmentation creates opportunities to compete through engineering, warranties, safety, software, financing, service and project execution.
It also explains why CATL’s overwhelming cell-market position does not automatically translate into system dominance.
GWh-Scale Projects Become the Next Battleground
Market leadership will increasingly depend on executing very large projects.
BYD’s 15.1 GWh Saudi cooperation demonstrates its ability to compete at enormous scale. CATL already has batteries deployed across approximately 2,300 storage projects.
Tesla says more than 77 GWh of Megapack storage is operational globally.
Meanwhile, the emergence of multi-GWh battery storage projects means utilities increasingly expect suppliers to provide more than batteries. They need engineering, commissioning, monitoring, warranties, augmentation and service for assets operating over many years.
That gives companies with manufacturing capacity, strong balance sheets and international service networks an advantage.
The Cost Battle Moves Beyond Battery Prices
CATL can use manufacturing scale to drive battery economics. BYD can potentially capture system-level efficiencies through vertical integration. Tesla is attempting to increase the revenue generated by each deployed asset through software.
The cheapest battery therefore does not necessarily create the lowest-cost BESS.
Developers need to consider efficiency, degradation, augmentation, availability, land requirements, warranties, financing and operating revenue.
Understanding BESS project costs in 2026 is increasingly important because battery cells represent only one part of total project investment.
The more meaningful measures are installed cost per usable kWh, lifetime energy throughput and risk-adjusted cash flow.
Who Leads Global Energy Storage in 2026?
The data produce three different winners.
CATL is the battery-scale leader. Its 22 percent H1 2026 cell share, 772 GWh manufacturing capacity at the end of 2025, technology breadth and approximately 2,300 deployed storage projects give it the strongest upstream position.
BYD is the system-integration leader. Its 9.1 percent system share put it first globally, while 96.6 percent shipment growth gives it the strongest momentum of the three companies.
Tesla is the software-led challenger. Megapack combined with Autobidder gives Tesla a differentiated proposition for projects where electricity-market participation and dispatch optimization materially affect revenue.
If one company must be identified as the broadest BESS leader in 2026, CATL has the strongest claim because its position combines battery manufacturing, R&D, technology breadth, global deployment and a growing system business.
But BYD is challenging CATL where the industry is increasingly creating value: complete storage systems.
Tesla faces the greatest market-share pressure, but its strategy is different. Rather than winning primarily through volume, it is attempting to capture more value from each installed GWh through standardized Megapack hardware and energy-market software.
The global BESS contest can therefore be summarized simply: CATL leads the battery layer, BYD leads the system layer, and Tesla is strongest at the software-intelligence layer.
The long-term winner will be the company capable of combining all three — low-cost battery technology, bankable system integration and software that maximizes the lifetime economic value of every GWh deployed.
SHAFANA FAZAL

articles.title: Tesla Megapack vs CATL TENER vs BYD MC Cube: Which BESS Offers the Best Technology and Project Economics? - GreentechLead
articles.summary: Tesla Megapack vs CATL TENER vs BYD MC Cube: Which BESS Offers the Best Technology and Project Economics?  GreentechLead
articles.full_text:
Tesla Megapack, CATL TENER and BYD MC Cube are competing for a rapidly expanding utility-scale battery energy storage system (BESS) market, but their strategies differ significantly.
Tesla emphasizes factory-integrated hardware, deployment and energy-market optimization through Autobidder. CATL is pushing container energy density, long-duration efficiency and lifecycle performance. BYD combines Blade Battery technology, Cell-to-System integration and vertically integrated LFP manufacturing.
For utilities and renewable-energy developers, however, the key question is not which company has the largest battery container. It is which BESS can deliver the lowest risk-adjusted lifetime cost and highest revenue from a project’s available land and grid connection.
There is no credible public evidence that Tesla, CATL or BYD universally offers the lowest installed cost or highest ROI. Project bids, EPC scope, warranties, grid connection and revenue models are needed to determine that.
This distinction becomes increasingly important as the world’s largest battery storage projects move from hundreds of MWh into multi-GWh territory.
Tesla Megapack: Software Could Be Its Biggest Advantage
Tesla’s four-hour Megapack configuration provides 979 kW of power and 3,916 kWh of energy per unit, with published round-trip efficiency of 93.7 percent. Its two-hour configuration provides 1,927 kW/3,854 kWh and 92 percent efficiency.
Megapack is factory integrated with battery modules, inverters and thermal systems and ships ready for installation.
The differentiator is increasingly software.
Tesla’s Autobidder uses price, load and generation forecasting to automate bidding and dispatch in wholesale electricity markets. Tesla says Autobidder-optimized sites cover more than 30 projects and 10 GWh and can also be offered with revenue guarantees.
That gives Tesla an important proposition for merchant BESS developers: combining hardware, servicing and revenue optimization.
Tesla is also expanding manufacturing. Megapack 3 production is scheduled at Megafactory Houston during 2026 with planned manufacturing capacity of up to 50 GWh annually.
Tesla advantage: standardized deployment plus a mature software and energy-trading layer.
CATL TENER: Energy Density and Efficiency Lead the Pitch
CATL has taken a different route by aggressively increasing the amount of energy that can be installed within a constrained site.
The original TENER stores 6.25 MWh in a 20-foot container, using LFP cells with energy density of 430 Wh/L. CATL says the design increases energy density per unit area by 30 percent and reduces station footprint by 20 percent.
CATL also claims TENER can achieve zero capacity and power degradation during its first five years under specified conditions. Developers need to evaluate the precise warranty and operating conditions behind that claim.
TENER H pushes capacity to 9,008 kWh per container and supports two-, four- and eight-hour configurations. CATL says the four- and eight-hour versions achieve round-trip efficiency of up to 96 percent, while increasing land utilization by 45 percent.
CATL also reported 125 GWh of ESS battery shipments during H1 2026, according to SNE Research data cited by the company.
CATL advantage: high energy density, manufacturing scale and long-duration configurations.
BYD MC Cube-T: Blade Battery Meets System Integration
BYD’s MC Cube-T combines the company’s LFP Blade Battery technology with Cell-to-System architecture.
MC Cube-T provides 6.432 MWh of capacity. BYD says the system reduces the number of parts and components by 36 percent while increasing space utilization by 98 percent.
The technology is already moving into large projects. A 100 MW/400 MWh project in Central California using BYD MC Cube entered service in 2025.
BYD also signed contracts with Saudi Electricity Company covering 12.5 GWh of grid-scale storage projects in 2025, taking their combined cooperation to 15.1 GWh including an earlier 2.6 GWh project.
MC Cube-T is no longer BYD’s highest-capacity platform. Its Haohan platform reaches up to 14.5 MWh, illustrating the rapid increase in container-level energy density.
BYD advantage: Blade Battery technology, vertical integration, CTS architecture and growing deployment scale.
The scale of these platforms reflects the broader energy storage investment boom as utilities and renewable-energy developers increasingly treat BESS as core grid infrastructure.
What Would a 200 MWh Project Require?
Container capacity illustrates how architecture affects the number of major battery units required.
| Platform | Energy per unit | Approx. units for 200 MWh | 
| Tesla Megapack 4-hour | 3.916 MWh | ~52 | 
| CATL TENER | 6.25 MWh | 32 | 
| BYD MC Cube-T | 6.432 MWh | ~32 | 
| CATL TENER H | 9.008 MWh | ~23 | 
These are simple energy-capacity calculations, not complete BESS designs.
A real project must account for PCS configuration, redundancy, usable capacity, safety separation, transformers, access roads, augmentation and interconnection.
Nevertheless, fewer battery units can potentially mean fewer foundations, cable runs and installation interfaces and a smaller overall footprint.
For developers comparing project economics, battery storage costs in 2026 increasingly depend on much more than the price of cells or containers.
CATL Leads on Published Container Density
For land-constrained projects, CATL’s TENER H is notable because it reaches approximately 9 MWh per container. BYD MC Cube-T’s 6.432 MWh is also substantially above Tesla’s published approximately 3.9 MWh four-hour Megapack configuration.
But container MWh alone should not determine procurement.
Tesla integrates the inverter within Megapack, so comparing battery-container capacity alone can exaggerate differences between architectures. Developers need to compare total plant footprint for the same MW/MWh specification.
The relevant commercial metric is ultimately usable MWh per acre, not simply MWh per container.
Efficiency can also have a substantial lifetime impact. Tesla publishes 93.7 percent round-trip efficiency for its four-hour Megapack, while CATL says four- and eight-hour TENER H configurations can achieve up to 96 percent.
However, developers must ensure efficiency figures use equivalent boundaries and testing conditions before making direct comparisons.
Tesla vs CATL vs BYD: Different Routes to ROI
Battery hardware is only one part of project ROI.
Tesla’s strongest economic argument is Autobidder. A merchant BESS must continuously decide whether electricity should be stored, discharged or held for another market opportunity. Tesla’s software can participate in wholesale energy, ancillary-service and capacity markets while optimizing dispatch.
For merchant projects, that capability may have more impact on lifetime returns than having the highest MWh per container.
CATL’s proposition becomes particularly strong where land availability and long-duration storage matter. Higher container capacity can potentially reduce the number of containers and balance-of-system interfaces.
BYD’s strength is vertical integration. Its Blade Battery and CTS approach reduces intermediate components while the company brings experience across battery cells, power electronics and integrated energy systems.
Supplier scale also affects bankability. Manufacturing capacity, delivery schedules, service networks and the financial ability to honor long-term warranties can be as important as headline battery specifications.
Which BESS Is Cheapest?
There is currently no defensible universal answer.
Battery-pack benchmarks should not be confused with delivered BESS prices. A utility-scale project also requires PCS, transformers, switchgear, fire protection, civil works, EPC, commissioning and grid connection.
The sharp decline in global battery energy storage system costs is improving the economics of all three platforms, but project-specific engineering and grid costs remain critical.
Developers should request bids using identical specifications and compare installed $/usable kWh, $/kW, efficiency, guaranteed availability, degradation, augmentation, warranty, O&M, footprint and lifetime throughput.
Which BESS Could Offer the Best ROI?
| Project priority | Platform to examine | Why | 
| Merchant optimization | Tesla | Autobidder + integrated hardware/software | 
| High container density | CATL | TENER H reaches ~9 MWh | 
| Long-duration storage | CATL | 4/8-hour configurations | 
| Blade Battery/CTS | BYD | Vertically integrated architecture | 
| Automated trading | Tesla | Autobidder | 
| Large-scale procurement | All three | GWh-scale capability | 
| Lowest CAPEX | Cannot determine publicly | Requires comparable bids | 
| Highest ROI | Cannot determine publicly | Depends on CAPEX and revenue | 
Bottom Line: Tesla, CATL and BYD Compete on Different Economics
Tesla Megapack, CATL TENER and BYD MC Cube should not be evaluated simply by asking which company sells the cheapest battery.
Tesla’s strongest differentiation is integrated hardware, deployment, service and revenue-optimization software.
CATL’s advantage is energy density, long-duration performance and enormous battery-manufacturing scale.
BYD combines Blade Battery technology, CTS integration, vertical manufacturing and experience delivering increasingly large BESS projects.
CATL currently has an advantage in this comparison on published container energy density, while Tesla has the clearest integrated proposition around merchant-market optimization. BYD provides a strong alternative for developers prioritizing vertically integrated LFP technology and system-level integration.
For utilities, developers and investors, the final procurement decision should compare installed cost per usable kWh, efficiency, degradation guarantees, augmentation, land requirement, availability, O&M, safety, financing and expected revenue.

articles.title: Pentagon’s Laser-Mesh Satellite Network Gains 21 Northrop Grumman Nodes - Tech Times
articles.summary: Pentagon’s Laser-Mesh Satellite Network Gains 21 Northrop Grumman Nodes  Tech Times
articles.full_text:
A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket deposited 21 Northrop Grumman-built satellites into low Earth orbit on Monday morning, the fourth time production spacecraft have reached orbit as part of the U.S. military's emerging laser-linked data network — a constellation the Pentagon intends to hand to Indo-Pacific commanders as an initial warfighting capability in early 2027.
The Tranche 1 Transport Layer Alpha (T1TL-A) mission lifted off from Space Launch Complex 4 East at Vandenberg Space Force Base, California, at 8:36 a.m. ET on Monday, one day after unfavorable weather forced a scrub of Sunday's attempt. The spacecraft were built for the Space Development Agency (SDA), the Space Force office responsible for populating what the Pentagon calls the Proliferated Warfighter Space Architecture (PWSA) — a network of hundreds of affordable, laser-crosslinked satellites designed to replace a handful of expensive, high-value spacecraft with a constellation so dense that no adversary counterspace strike could knock all of it out at once.
Northrop Grumman's First Tranche 1 Spacecraft Reach Orbit
Monday's mission carries particular significance for Northrop Grumman: the 21 satellites aboard represent the company's first Tranche 1 Transport Layer spacecraft to reach orbit, after the program worked through a succession of supply-chain delays that pushed the original September 2024 launch timeline back by roughly a year.
The SDA awarded Northrop Grumman, Lockheed Martin, and York Space Systems a combined $1.8 billion contract in early 2022 to build 126 Transport Layer satellites in total, with Northrop's share covering 42 spacecraft. To build them quickly and cheaply, Northrop partnered with Airbus, which supplied satellite buses derived from the same commercial Arrow platform used for OneWeb's broadband satellite constellation — a deliberate SDA strategy of leveraging commercial production rates for military hardware.
Each satellite carries two key payload types: Link 16 tactical datalinks and Optical Inter-Satellite Links (OISLs). Together, they are what transform individual satellites into a true military network.
What Are Optical Inter-Satellite Links, and Why Do They Matter?
An Optical Inter-Satellite Link, or OISL, is a laser communication channel between satellites — no radio waves, no spectrum license, no ground station in the loop. The carrier is a near-infrared laser operating at 1,550 nanometers (the same wavelength used by terrestrial fiber-optic networks), and demonstrated data rates range from roughly 1.8 gigabits per second on early operational systems to more than 100 gigabits per second on advanced research payloads.
The practical consequence is dramatic. Traditional radio-frequency crosslinks between satellites typically top out at 50 to 200 megabits per second and require spectrum licensing through international regulators. An OISL terminal, by contrast, can carry an order of magnitude more data with no licensing overhead and near-zero risk of jamming or interception — because the beam spreads only a few meters wide by the time it reaches a peer satellite, meaning an adversary would have to physically insert a receiver into that narrow beam in space to intercept it.
More fundamentally, OISLs eliminate the ground-station bottleneck. Without them, every satellite needs line-of-sight to a ground station to move data — so a satellite over the Pacific serves no one unless it can reach a teleport somewhere beneath it. With OISLs, traffic routes satellite-to-satellite across the constellation, crossing oceans and continents without ever touching the atmosphere, until it descends to a user who needs it. That is what makes a "proliferated LEO architecture" function as a network rather than a fleet of isolated spacecraft.
The Open Standard That Makes Multi-Vendor Networking Possible
None of this works if satellites built by different companies cannot link to each other. The SDA addressed this early by publishing an open Optical Communications Terminal (OCT) standard — a common protocol that all PWSA vendors must build to.
That standard was validated in January 2025, when York Space Systems and SpaceX demonstrated the first inter-vendor, inter-layer laser communications link on orbit — a Tranche 0 data transport satellite built by York successfully closing a laser link with a Tranche 0 missile tracking satellite built by SpaceX. "Achieving the first inter-vendor, inter-layer laser link demonstrates the tangible value of open standards and collaborative efforts in rapidly achieving an integrated space architecture," York CEO Dirk Wallinger said at the time.
The OCT standard is also at the center of a larger contest about who will control the future language of the space-based internet. Laser terminal suppliers publicly named for PWSA Tranche 1 include Mynaric, Tesat Spacecom, and Skyloom. The SDA is pushing hard for its open spec to become the common language for U.S. government and commercial systems alike — a fight that will determine whether the Pentagon's space-based network eventually interoperates with commercial constellations or operates as an isolated government island.
What Is Link 16 Doing in Space?
The Link 16 payload aboard each PWSA satellite is a forty-year-old technology being asked to do something new. Link 16 is the NATO standard tactical data link that enables aircraft, warships, and ground forces to share a synchronized picture of the battlefield in near-real time — using radio frequencies between 960 and 1,215 MHz, it is a jam-resistant, time-division-multiplexed network that has been the backbone of NATO air operations since the 1980s. Its one historical limitation: range is restricted to line-of-sight, making intercontinental relay impossible.
Mounting Link 16 terminals on a satellite at 750 to 1,200 kilometers (466 to 746 miles) in altitude extends that range to roughly 3,146 nautical miles (5,826 kilometers) — intercontinental, and essentially global when the full constellation is populated. This is the mechanism behind the SDA's stated goal of enabling "beyond-line-of-sight targeting": PWSA relays Link 16 data through the orbital mesh, giving commanders and shooters a shared tactical picture that does not depend on where they are relative to friendly ground infrastructure.
Each Tranche 1 satellite also integrates with the Integrated Broadcast System (IBS), enabling threat warnings and situational awareness to reach commanders at the tactical edge. The full architecture represents what the Pentagon calls Joint All-Domain Command and Control (JADC2) — connecting sensors, decision-makers, and shooters across air, sea, land, space, and cyber domains into a unified, time-compressed kill chain enabling rapid military response.
A Constellation Built in Waves
T1TL-A is the fourth production mission for the PWSA, following three earlier launches that began populating the Tranche 1 architecture:
- T1TL-B (September 10, 2025) — 21 York Space Systems satellites
- T1TL-C (October 15, 2025) — 21 Lockheed Martin satellites
- T1TL-E (July 16, 2026) — 21 York Space Systems satellites
With 63 Tranche 1 Transport Layer satellites already in orbit from those prior missions, Monday's addition of 21 Northrop Grumman spacecraft brings the total to approximately 84 Tranche 1 satellites on orbit — roughly two-thirds of the 126 Transport Layer spacecraft the full constellation requires. The missions, while labeled alphabetically, have not launched in that sequence. As Space Force Col. Ryan Hiserote, division chief in the Assured Access to Space directorate at Space Systems Command, explained in September 2025: "The first three missions (A, B, and C) as to their order of launches are interchangeable."
When the Transport Layer is complete and laser links are operating, the SDA has said 95 percent of the globe will be in view of at least two satellites at any given time, operating over Ka band at altitudes between 750 and 1,200 kilometers (466 to 746 miles).
How Does Low Orbit Beat Geostationary Satellites for Military Use?
A traditional military communications satellite parked in geostationary orbit (GEO) sits at 35,786 kilometers (22,236 miles) above Earth, where it can see a third of the globe from a fixed spot. The distance alone introduces about 250 milliseconds of one-way signal delay — a half-second round trip. At that latency, a pilot trying to receive a missile-warning update is receiving yesterday's picture.
PWSA satellites at 750 to 1,200 kilometers (466 to 746 miles) cut that distance by a factor of thirty, reducing one-way latency to roughly three to five milliseconds. The tradeoff is coverage: a single LEO satellite crosses the sky in minutes, so you need hundreds of them to maintain persistent global coverage. That is precisely the calculation the SDA has made — proliferating affordable spacecraft and weaving them into a mesh to replicate and exceed what any individual high-value GEO satellite can do, while being far harder for an adversary to eliminate in a single strike.
The GAO's Standing Concerns — and the Standards Problem Beneath Them
The Government Accountability Office has issued two reports raising concerns about the SDA's pace of OISL demonstration. A February 2025 report found that the agency had not sufficiently demonstrated laser communication capabilities on its Tranche 0 satellites before proceeding with Tranche 1 launches, warning that "this technology is much more complex" than traditional radio-frequency satellite communications. A January 2026 follow-on report found that SDA was overestimating technology readiness of critical components and lacked an architecture-level schedule.
As of the SATELLITE 2026 conference in March, SDA Director Gurpartap Sandhoo confirmed the agency was approximately three months behind schedule on its OISL demonstration goals — while maintaining that the delay would not prevent initial warfighting capability from reaching INDOPACOM in early 2027. articles.title: SpaceX T1TL-A Launch Scrubbed: 21 SDA Satellites Explained - Techgenyz
articles.summary: SpaceX T1TL-A Launch Scrubbed: 21 SDA Satellites Explained  Techgenyz
articles.full_text:
SpaceX scrubbed the October 5 launch attempt after the countdown was halted at about T−58 seconds, preventing the Falcon 9 from carrying out its planned mission for the U.S. Space Development Agency (SDA). The mission, known as Tranche 1 Transport Layer A (T1TL-A), was scheduled to launch from Space Launch Complex 4E at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California at 08:17 UTC. SpaceX is now targeting October 6 at 08:17 UTC for another launch attempt, although schedules remain subject to change. The reason for the October 5 countdown halt remains unconfirmed unless SpaceX provides an official update.
The important part of this mission, however, goes beyond the delayed launch. The 21 satellites are part of the Proliferated Warfighter Space Architecture (PWSA), a distributed low-Earth-orbit network being developed to provide faster and more resilient space-based communications and data services. Unlike a commercial broadband satellite launch, these spacecraft are designed around military data transport and connectivity.
What the 21 Satellites Are Designed to Do
The T1TL-A spacecraft belong specifically to the Transport Layer of SDA’s Tranche 1 architecture. Tranche 1 as a whole supports regional military communications, advanced missile warning and tracking, and beyond-line-of-sight targeting. The Transport Layer primarily provides the low-latency communications network that moves data between sensors and users. The separate Tracking Layer carries infrared sensing payloads for missile warning and tracking.
In simple terms, the Transport Layer satellites are designed to act as nodes in a network in space. Rather than concentrating capability in a small number of spacecraft, PWSA distributes functions across a proliferated constellation of smaller satellites. This approach is intended to improve resilience, scalability, and low-latency connectivity.
SDA says the Transport Layer spacecraft include Link 16 tactical data-link capability, Ka-band RF communications and optical communications terminals. These systems allow the satellites to connect with other spacecraft, ground systems and relevant warfighter platforms.
The T1TL-A mission is carrying 21 satellites manufactured by Northrop Grumman. Before this mission, three successful Tranche 1 Transport Layer launches had already placed 63 satellites into orbit. SDA confirmed that the third launch on July 16, 2026, brought the total number of on-orbit Tranche 1 spacecraft to 63.
What Optical Links Matter
One of the most important technologies behind the network is optical communication. Each Tranche 1 spacecraft is configured with optical communication terminals that support satellite-to-satellite and satellite-to-ground optical communications.
SDA says the combination of low-Earth orbit and optical inter-satellite links is designed to provide low-latency data transport, while optical links offer performance advantages over traditional RF crosslinks. This is important for a network intended to move time-sensitive information across space.
The optically interconnected Transport Layer is designed as a mesh network that can move data across the constellation and deliver it to warfighter platforms. This means the satellites are being developed as connected nodes within a larger communications architecture rather than as isolated spacecraft.
A Distributed Military Network in Low Earth Orbit
PWSA is being built around a proliferated constellation of satellites operating in low Earth orbit. SDA describes the Transport Layer as a dynamically networked constellation designed to provide assured, resilient, and low-latency military data and connectivity. The wider Transport Layer is envisioned to eventually include hundreds of satellites.
For Tranche 1 specifically, the planned operational constellation consists of 154 spacecraft — 126 Transport Layer satellites and 28 Tracking Layer satellites — plus four missile-defense demonstration spacecraft. The Transport Layer handles communications and data transport, while the Tracking Layer uses infrared sensing payloads for missile warning and tracking.
This distinction is important because the 21 satellites aboard T1TL-A are Transport Layer spacecraft. They do not themselves perform the primary missile-sensing function. Instead, they are designed to provide the communications network that can transport information from sensing systems to users and warfighter platforms.
The proliferated, dynamically networked architecture is designed to provide greater fault tolerance and alternative paths when individual nodes become unavailable. SDA describes the Transport Layer as a resilient, dynamically networked system with greater bandwidth and fault tolerance.
What Happens Next for T1TL-A?
The October 5 scrub occurred before liftoff, so nothing was launched, and there was no in-flight rocket failure. SpaceX is now targeting October 6 at 08:17 UTC for another attempt, although the schedule can still change. The reason for the October 5 countdown halt should not be assumed unless SpaceX officially confirms it.
When T1TL-A eventually launches, its significance will extend beyond adding 21 spacecraft to orbit. The mission will expand the PWSA’s Tranche 1 Transport Layer, adding another group of satellites to the existing network. The broader architecture is intended to transport military communications and data, including information supporting missile warning, tracking, and targeting missions.
Conclusion
The October 5 countdown scrub delayed an important step in the Space Development Agency’s growing satellite network, but it does not change the mission’s broader significance. The 21 T1TL-A satellites are designed to strengthen low-Earth-orbit communications through interconnected spacecraft, optical links, and faster data transport. Once launched, they will expand the PWSA’s Tranche 1 Transport Layer and contribute to a distributed, resilient space-based network that transports military communications and data, including information supporting missile warning, tracking and targeting missions.

articles.summary: The tool can free up over 12GB of storage.
articles.full_text:
A new tool is allowing Mac users the ability again to easily turn off Apple Intelligence with one click and free up to 12GB of storage.
Unlike with previous versions of macOS, macOS 27 Golden Gate doesn’t have a toggle for turning off Apple Intelligence. That makes disabling AI features that you may not want more difficult. It also means that the AI models necessary for running Apple Intelligence will take up space on your disk, even if you don’t use them or if you go through your settings to individually find and disable AI capabilities.
In response, a developer known as Om Lahore on GitHub last week created RemoveMacAI, a command-line tool that allows macOS 27 users to “turn off Apple Intelligence on macOS 27" in a way that is “fully reversible,” per the GitHub page. They said that Apple's Intelligence models take up "about 12GB," but the models can actually take up over 30GB, The Verge noted.Read full article

articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 06 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03092-1Francis Halzen wins the 2026 award for his work on a neutrino observatory at the South Pole that has helped to unlock mysteries of the Universe.

Belgian-born physicist Francis Halzen has won the 2026 Nobel Prize on Physics for his work in detecting high-energy elusive particles called neutrinos that come from deep in space.
His pioneering contribution is the founding of a giant detector, the IceCube Neutrino Observatory, at the South Pole. Its results have helped to found the fields of neutrino and multimessenger astronomy, which help physicists to unlock the mysteries of the Universe through observing highly energetic events from deep in the cosmos.
Halzen, who is based at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, takes home all of the 12-million Swedish kronor (US$1.2-million) prize, announced by the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in Stockholm on 6 October. It is the first time since 1992 that the the physics prize has been awarded to only one winner.
“It was a great surprise and I obviously didn’t expect it,” said Halzen, speaking to the Nobel press conference after the prize was announced. “This reflects on the really courageous people who joined me in this project when really no respectable conservative physicist would have joined me, but many talented people did and that’s why I’m here.”
Neutrinos are the second most common particle in the Universe, after photons. More than 1 billion neutrinos pass through a hand every second, but high-energy neutrinos are extremely rare and hard to detect. IceCube was designed to study the particles when they fly out of some of the most energetic environments in the Universe, such as supernovae and γ-ray bursts. Because neutrinos pass straight through matter, they provide a straight line back to these events, providing researchers with a unique way of probing astrophysical phenomena.
Halzen is “a father figure for neutrino astronomy”, says Paschal Coyle, a neutrino physicist at Aix-Marseille University in France and the spokesperson of KM3NeT, a similarly large observatory being built in the Mediterranean Sea.
Looking into the cosmos
Despite being all around us, neutrinos are fiendishly difficult to detect because they are unaffected by magnetic fields and rarely ever interact. In the 1980s, Halzen had the idea to use threads of detectors, lowered more than 1.5 kilometres into holes drilled into the clear ice of the Antarctic — which is free from many types of interference — to detect the rare and faint flashes of light when a fast-moving neutrino hits an atom.
As long as the volume was big enough, Halzen theorized that the set-up could catch neutrinos and the path would reveal the direction from which they come, allowing researchers to trace their origins in the cosmos (see ‘Neutrino observatory’).
The IceCube Neutrino Observatory — an array of 5,160 sensors — was completed in 2011 at a cost of US$271 million, funded by the US National Science Foundation. It now involves a collaboration of more than 450 researchers. “After one and a half decades of development, and another decade of construction, there was no guarantee we would ever see anything,” Halzen, principal investigator of IceCube, told APS news in 2025. “Many people thought we wouldn’t, but we did.”
Within two years, the detector had observed neutrinos from beyond the galaxy and with extreme energies. In 2013, IceCube published a result1 showing that there was a population of neutrinos at energies so high that could not have been produced anywhere in the Solar System, and establishing the new field of neutrino astronomy.
“The biggest risk we took is that nobody knew if the kilometer cube detector was actually large enough to detect neutrinos beyond our atmosphere from the Universe and that was our biggest one. But it only took two years to detect that,” Halzen told the Nobel press conference.
“We found evidence for neutrinos coming from supermassive black holes in other galaxies, and they shine so strongly that when you look at a neutrino sky you don’t see the Milky Way.”
In 2014, IceCube discovered three neutrinos with energies that blew all others out of the water. Nicknamed Bert, Ernie and Big Bird, they had energies on the scale of petaelectronvolts, thousands of times more energetic than those produced in Earth’s most advanced particle colliders. And three years later, the collaboration made a long-awaited discovery of a high-energy neutrino that they could for the first time trace back to a specific source — a distant galaxy, called TXS 0506+056, often referred to as ‘the Texas event’.
Follow-up observations suggested that the source was a ‘blazar’, a violent galaxy harbouring a supermassive black hole at its core, that can flare up in brightness. Studies from a suite of telescopes viewing the blazar using different methods described the source across seven papers in 2018.
‘Undisputed force’
Halzen was born in Tienen in Belgium in 1944 and studied at the country’s University of Louvain in Ottignies-Louvain-la-Neuve. He trained as a particle physicist, working at CERN, Europe’s particle-physics laboratory near Geneva, Switzerland, before moving to Wisconsin in 1971.

articles.full_text:
Today marks the worldwide launch of Gears of War: E-Day, now available on XBOX Series X|S, XBOX on PC, Game Pass and Steam. One of XBOX’s most iconic sagas returns to where it all began, taking players back to the opening hours of Emergence Day and the catastrophic event that changed the world of Sera forever.
Emergence Day is a defining moment for the Gears of War universe – the catastrophic event changed the world of Sera forever, but the story of that fateful night has never been fully told, until now.
Gears of War: E-Day transports us back to the opening hours of the Locust invasion, where an unsuspecting world is ruthlessly plunged into chaos as monsters erupt from underground. Across three harrowing days and nights, Marcus Fenix, Dom Santiago and their fierce new squad mates fight desperately to survive the onslaught consuming the city of Kalona, while uncovering the true scale of a threat unlike anything they – or humanity – has ever faced.
From the moment the prologue opens, Gears of War: E-Day showcases a masterclass in action-horror. This is not the Locust enemy you’ve fought before. They’re equally cunning as they are violent, and frankly, you should be terrified to face them. If this is your first deployment, or you’re coming out of retirement to fight the war ahead, we’ve got you covered. Before you step out onto the streets of Kalona, here are a few things every Gear should know.
Learn When to Push Forward, When to Hold Your Ground, and When to Get Out of the F**ckin’ Way
Gears of War is famously a cover-based shooter, and you’ll rely on it to stay alive as you push through the Locust. Keep your head down and dip from cover-to-cover – and avoid walking out into the open unless you’re rushing an enemy with a melee attack. Even a handful of Drones can deal massive damage while you’re exposed, which can be trouble for both you and the squadmate that may have to come and revive you. Sometimes, the best course of action is to hold patiently and pick off enemies as they come, and there’s no shame in that strategy.
Sometimes, you’ll just need to haul ass and stay as mobile as you can, which I quickly learned during an early fight with a Brumak wielding a horrible chain weapon. There’s no peace to be found in cover for that situation – fan out, keep it distracted, and pray that it doesn’t decide to charge you while your gun is jammed.
Know Your Loadout
Each weapon you’ll find in E-Day is deeply situational, which makes for a great tactical experience. The Chainsaw Lancer is a great all-rounder, offering close-to-mid range firepower and a big ol’ (upgradeable) mag to chew through. The Gnasher is a stellar shotgun, fantastic for devastating point-blank damage. The Longshot Sniper, one of my personal favorites, pops a slick, long-range slug into unsuspecting foes from a great distance. Not only is that incredibly satisfying each time, but it lets you get a stack of damage into a tankier enemy – like a Boomer, before it gets close to you. There are caches dotted around Kalona that let you switch up your loadout, too, so don’t feel like you’re locked into a specific style of play forever. Mix up your strategy, swap roles with your friends, but above all – experiment!
Melee is a Gear’s Best Friend
I know I said this is a cover-based shooter, but sometimes you’ll need to resort to more personal measures. Before E-Day even lets you look at a gun, it hands out a crash course in melee – one of the most useful, life-saving abilities for a Gear. Spend some time getting to grips with how it works when wielding a metal pipe and the Snub pistol – figure out the weight of the swing, and how it feels to hit enemies in front, and more importantly, behind you. Later, melee becomes even more fun with the Chainsaw Lancer, and you’ll feel extra confident with it once you’ve got the basics of backhanding down.
Blind Shooting is Back, and Remains Effective
As soon as you pop your head up to aim a shot, you’re a giant bullet magnet, effectively inviting every weapon-wielder on the map to pop you like a balloon. Fortunately, Gears can shoot blind from behind cover, which is a superb way to dish out additional damage to something getting too close for comfort. If you don’t have the health to rush out for a melee takedown, or you need a few seconds of recovery time, blind fire from cover is a clutch move to get the job done.
Look Out For Side Missions, And Their Rewards
While E-Day‘s campaign is primarily linear, Kalona has large pockets of open space with multiple pathways towards the next objective, as well as side paths that may lead to side missions. These are smaller, optional objectives that let you support other squads, help civilians, and otherwise contribute to saving the city. Not only do they offer additional insight into the wider story, you’ll also get a nice reward for doing it, often a weapon mod.
Audio Chime Means Collectables
While you’re exploring, keep an ear open for a sharp chime whenever you enter a new area of the city – anywhere from inside a building to a side street. That means there’s a collectable nearby. These range from familiar items like COG armor and tags, to esoteric pieces like… a can of soup. They all come with great little lore entries too, some written by the squad members themselves. It’s a wonderful added insight into their stories, and the wider world, so pick them up when you can.
Now that you’re equipped with the basics, there’s only one thing left to do – get out there. Gather your squad, load up, and uncover the world-shattering event that started it all. articles.summary: Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA), Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL) And Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) Now Represent Over 21% Of The S&P 500  Foreign Policy Journal
articles.full_text:
The S&P 500 has reached an unprecedented level of concentration, with just three technology giants now accounting for more than a fifth of the entire index.
Data from Creative Planning shows that Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA), Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL), and Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) collectively represent over 21% of the S&P 500 (INDEXSP: .INX), a record high level of combined weighting.
To put that dominance in historical perspective, IBM (NYSE: IBM), AT&T, and ExxonMobil at their peak in the mid-1980s made up just 13.4% of the S&P 500.
The concentration of these three stocks has intensified over the past month, driven by a series of favorable corporate developments that have pushed share prices higher across all three companies.
Nvidia ignited investor enthusiasm two weeks ago when it revealed a $150 billion stock buyback plan, described as the largest share repurchase authorization increase in history.
That announcement brings Nvidia’s total buyback authorization to $235 billion, signaling extraordinary confidence from management in the company’s financial position and future earnings power.
Nvidia shares are now hovering near a record high, reinforcing the company’s status as the dominant force in artificial intelligence chip design and supply.
Apple’s stock is trading near its own record high, fueled by strong investor reaction to the company’s product unveiling event held in mid-September.
The centerpiece of that event was the iPhone Duo, a passport-like folding device featuring a 5.4-inch front display that expands to a 7.6-inch screen when opened, designed for movies, gaming, and multitasking.
Apple also introduced the new iPhone 18 suite and updated AirPods at the same event, broadening the product refresh cycle heading into the critical holiday quarter.
Microsoft’s stock has also pushed ahead in recent weeks, even though the company has not produced the same volume of headline-grabbing announcements as its two peers.
Wall Street analysts have been raising earnings estimates for Microsoft for both this year and next, citing expectations that surging AI demand will translate into strong Azure cloud sales growth.
The record concentration of these three stocks within the S&P 500 underscores how heavily the broader market’s performance has become tied to the fortunes of a handful of technology companies.

articles.title: NEAR Intents Attacker Returns $3.8M as Nvidia AI Chip Smuggling Case Raises Security Concerns - Tekedia

articles.full_text:
$3.8 million stolen in a crypto exploit has been returned. At the same time, authorities are investigating an alleged $300 million operation to smuggle Nvidia’s most powerful AI chips into China.
As technology becomes more valuable, the battle to control, protect and profit from it is becoming more intense. In crypto, the latest development involving NEAR Intents offers a rare ending to an exploit story.
The attacker behind the incident has reportedly returned the full $3.8 million taken during the exploit. The recovery changes the immediate financial outcome for affected users, but it does not erase the vulnerabilities that made the attack possible.

For decentralized finance, every exploit is also a stress test of the systems responsible for moving assets across chains. NEAR Intents had previously frozen cross-chain swaps after a bug allowed funds to be drained.
The decision demonstrated an increasingly important principle in decentralized infrastructure: when an incident occurs, speed of containment can be as important as the technology itself.
The return of the funds is therefore significant not only because of the money recovered, but because it limits the permanent damage that could otherwise have been imposed on users and confidence in the protocol.
Yet the episode raises a difficult question. Should users have to depend on an attacker voluntarily returning stolen assets for a crisis to end well? The answer is clearly no. Protocols need stronger auditing, monitoring, transaction controls and incident-response mechanisms before capital is put at risk.
At the other end of the technology spectrum, an alleged $300 million Nvidia AI-chip smuggling scheme highlights a different kind of vulnerability. Earthmade Computers CEO Greg Lui has reportedly been arrested over allegations that advanced Nvidia chips were illegally moved to China.
The case underscores how AI hardware has evolved from ordinary commercial equipment into a strategic asset at the centre of the global technology competition. The importance of Nvidia’s accelerators extends beyond the semiconductor industry.
High-end GPUs provide much of the computational power required to train and operate increasingly sophisticated artificial-intelligence systems. As governments impose export controls on advanced chips, the hardware itself becomes part of a broader geopolitical contest involving national security, supply chains and technological sovereignty.
The alleged smuggling case illustrates the difficulty of enforcing those restrictions. Chips can move through intermediaries, shell companies, resellers and complex international supply chains, creating opportunities for restricted technology to reach markets where regulators intend to limit access.
A case involving hundreds of millions of dollars also demonstrates the economic incentives available to anyone willing to circumvent those controls. The two stories reveal two sides of the modern technology economy.
In decentralized finance, value can move globally at digital speed, creating opportunities for innovation while opening new attack surfaces. In artificial intelligence.
Physical computing infrastructure has become so strategically important that governments are increasingly treating advanced chips as controlled technology rather than ordinary commercial products.
The return of the $3.8 million NEAR Intents funds provides a positive outcome for users, but it should not become an excuse to overlook the underlying exploit. Likewise, the alleged Nvidia smuggling operation shows that export controls can only be effective when regulators can trace not just manufacturers.
But the entire chain through which advanced computing hardware changes hands. Both cases point toward the same conclusion: as technology becomes more valuable, the systems surrounding it must become more resilient.
Security, transparency and accountability are no longer secondary concerns. They are becoming fundamental infrastructure for the digital economy.
